steps.say: Pancreatic injuries are filed from one to five, from a simple bruise through a snapped body to a shattered head. The dividing line that matters is the main duct, because a cut duct never heals on its own. From grade three upward the duct is assumed involved, and those patients go to theatre. Lower grades can be watched.
steps.tx: **AAST** grades pancreatic injury **I to V** (one to five: contusion through distal transection to massive head disruption), with **ductal disruption** (divided main duct) from grade **III** upward mandating surgery. Grading standardises reports, and duct involvement overrules parenchymal grade in every borderline scan.

steps.say: Amylase blood tests mislead in the first hours, so a normal value never rules out a duct cut. The scan that finds the cut uses thin pancreatic phase slices, and an MRCP within a day maps the duct directly. Together they are the answer to the only question that counts, resection or drainage. The scans are repeated when the picture evolves.
steps.tx: Serum amylase misleads in the first hours, so phased-contrast CT with **pancreatic-phase CT** (thin arterial slices through the gland) plus **MRCP** (magnetic duct map) inside **24** hours hunts the duct cut that chooses resection over drainage. Re-scanning catches leaks that declare late.

steps.say: A clean snap left of the big vessels calls for removing the tail, and the spleen can usually stay. Keeping the spleen spares a young patient lifelong sepsis risk, so vessels are teased off the gland whenever stability allows. Rushing to remove the spleen is reserved for hilar bleeding or a clock running out.
steps.tx: A clean snap left of the mesenteric vessels earns spleen-preserving **distal pancreatectomy** (tail removal) when stable, with splenectomy only when hilar bleeding or time pressure dominates. **Spleen-preserving** (keeping the spleen with its vessels) technique avoids lifelong sepsis risk in the young for decades after.

steps.say: Head injuries are split by what survives. When the papilla and bile duct live on, the head is drained and the stomach outlet is closed with a bypass join, resting everything downstream. When the papilla is torn off or the duodenum is dead, patching is futile and the whole block comes out as a trauma Whipple.
steps.tx: Head-end injuries sparing ampulla and bile duct settle for drainage with **pyloric exclusion** (pylorus closed) and gastrojejunostomy, while ampullary avulsion or dead duodenum demands **trauma Whipple** (emergency pancreaticoduodenectomy removing the block). Duct and ampulla status decides the whole operation every time.

steps.say: A child folded over handlebars who cannot keep anything down usually has a bruised shut duodenum rather than a burst one. The treatment is a nose tube with ten to fourteen days of patience, confirmed by a dye study showing the passage open before feeding restarts. Operating on a bruise turns it into a leak.
steps.tx: **Duodenal haematoma** (bruised shut duodenum) blocking high after a blunt blow in childhood settles with **10 to 14** days of **nasogastric decompression** (stomach suction with gut rest), proven open by a contrast swallow before feeding resumes. Operation converts haematoma into leak.

steps.say: Small holes are sewn shut across the gut, never along it, with a patch of omentum tacked over the top. That rule holds for tears under half the circumference seen early. Ragged holes past three quarters, or any hole found late after contamination, need the bigger diversion operation with the outlet closed and a bypass join.
steps.tx: Duodenal perforation under **50** percent circumference gets primary **transverse closure** (across-gut suture avoiding narrowing) with **omental patch** (omentum tacked over the repair), while ragged holes past **75** percent or late presentations demand pyloric exclusion with a bypass join. Transverse lines always preserve the lumen calibre.

nodes.label: Under 50 percent and early, or over 75 percent and late

steps.say: Leaking pancreatic juice is measured before it is managed. Small leaks under two hundred millilitres a day dry up with octreotide and gut feeding in four out of five cases. Big gushers, or leaks still flowing past six weeks, need the duct stented from inside or the leaking segment removed. Volume and time set the ladder.
steps.tx: Post-traumatic fistula under **200** mL per day is closed by **octreotide** (secretion-slowing analogue) and enteral nutrition in **80** percent, while **high-output fistula** (large-volume leak) or leaks refusing to close by **6** weeks move to ERCP stenting or resection. Output volume guides the ladder.

rows: Octreotide plus gut feeds, closes in 80 percent

steps.say: A leak missed at the first operation returns weeks later as a painful cyst or a stubborn discharging sinus. Once the wall firms up at six weeks, the cyst is joined to the stomach from inside so it drains where it should. External drains placed too early simply create permanent tracks. Internal drainage cures.
steps.tx: **Missed injury** (unrecognised duct division) declares itself through pseudocyst or fistula weeks later, and is managed by internal drainage with **cystgastrostomy** (cyst joined to the stomach) once the wall matures at **6** weeks. Early external drainage recurs, and infected collections need external drainage first.
